summary.text:
A short annual outturn from a small Lancashire district running a General-Fund-only balance sheet at £83.2m CFR. External borrowing is not stated as a single figure in the paper — instead, movements are itemised: one new PWLB loan drawn (£7m 1-year at 4.62%, 18 March 2026) and £3.03m repaid (a £3m 1-year matured, plus £30k residual on a 1998 amortising loan). No LOBOs, market debt or LA short-term borrowing are named anywhere; the Tables 2 and 3 read as PWLB-only.

The reconciliation ties honestly on principal and on the cross-check that matters. Our file holds 31 PWLB loans for Burnley totalling £62.89m at a principal-weighted 2.7109%. The paper's own 2.64% average rate (§8, p.6) is 7 basis points lower — explained by methodology, since the paper's 2.64% is interest paid (£1,538,500) divided by average principal through the year (c.£58.3m), whereas ours is a snapshot rate weighted by principal at year end. The £7m 1-year PWLB drawn on 18 March 2026 at 4.62% reproduces exactly in our file as PW913692 — that's the tie that proves the reading.

The balance-sheet identity is our arithmetic on the paper's CFR: £83.2m CFR − £62.89m PWLB − £0 OLTL = £20.31m internal borrowing. Consistent with the paper's own §5.2 language ('under-borrowed position', 'cash supporting the Authority's reserves, balances and cash flow was used as an interim measure') and §10's £8.4m daily average of internally managed funds. If any non-PWLB debt exists that we don't see, the internal figure shrinks accordingly — nothing in this paper suggests it does.

Two things sit near the edge of interesting. First, £11m across three loans reprices inside twelve months (17.5% of the book), and the two rolling positions are already at 4.62% and 4.90%. Second, on the DMO's premature redemption curve at 14 August the 31-loan book prices to a £21.2m indicative discount (33.9% of principal), driven by two ANNUITY positions with 25-year+ tails at coupons of 2.15% and 2.22%. Both are internal context; the paper carries no rescheduling discussion, and §8 states 'No rescheduling was done during the year'. Meeting was 6 August 2026, already 9 days past. Next treasury touchpoint expected around September 2026 per the paper's stated cadence (Q1 to Executive). Draft written and addressed to the Principal Accountant named on the paper front sheet — this paper does not name a S151 by name.

officer.body:
Hi Craig,

Apologies for the cold email. PWLBtoday is fairly new so you may not have come across us yet.

We're built for local authority treasury teams and nothing else: live PWLB rates at both daily fixings, a monthly breakdown of every loan the sector draws, every council's PWLB book priced daily against the DMO's repayment curve, and a training academy for officers and members. There's more — the predictor, the SONIA path, peer metrics, a daily brief — in the brochure at [BROCHURE URL]. We don't sell treasury products, and the data side is free and stays free.

To keep that data and our training relevant we built tools that watch committee papers across every council in the country, so we can see how a council's own figures compare with where the market has gone since. So below are a few thoughts on the Annual Treasury Management Report that went to Full Council on 6 August. You're not being singled out — every authority gets one of these — and there's no agenda in it. The report is clear and well laid out and this is offered in that spirit, not as a critique.

A cross-check first. The £7m 1-year PWLB you drew on 18 March at 4.62% (§7 and Table 2) reproduces in our file loan-for-loan — PW913692, maturity 18 March 2027, £7,000,000, 4.62% on the Certainty rate. That's the tie that means the numbers below are pulled against your own paper rather than an aggregate.

Around it, our file holds 31 PWLB loans for Burnley totalling £62.89m at a principal-weighted 2.71%. Your paper prints 2.64% at paragraph 8 as the average rate on borrowed sums at 31 March. The 7 basis point gap is a methodology point — 2.64% is your £1,538,500 of interest payable divided by the roughly £58m of average principal outstanding through the year, and 2.71% is our snapshot rate weighted by principal at year end. Both are legitimate; yours is the more conservative reading against a book that has just added the 4.62% position. Worth flagging honestly rather than smoothing over.

On the balance-sheet side, the paper isn't asked to publish total external borrowing so it doesn't. Working the identity from your Table 1 CFR of £83.2m and our record of the £62.89m PWLB book (Tables 2 and 3 don't name any non-PWLB debt), that implies about £20.3m of internal borrowing — consistent with the language in paragraph 5.2 and the £8.4m daily average of internally managed funds at paragraph 10. If there's any non-PWLB stock we don't hold, the internal figure would come down by that amount.

The near-term shape is where the book has movement. About £11m across three PWLB loans reprices within twelve months — 17.5% of the total — the £7m you just drew, a £3m at 4.90% maturing on 12 March 2027, and a smaller £1m position at a much lower coupon. Your paragraph 5.2 spells out the deliberate short-dated cashflow-support policy, so this isn't a surprise, but the mechanical repricing is real for a book of this size. On yesterday's Certainty fixing (PWLB notice 314/26 PM, 14 August) the 1-year is 4.95% and Bank Rate is still 3.75%.

Which is why I'd point you to pwlbtoday.org/pwlb-activity. The monthly sector data shows what the PWLB is actually lending, at what rate and to whom, so you can see whether the market is thinning or opening before you roll. July was £368m across 33 loans from 19 borrowers at an average 5.02% — a quiet month. The daily-priced view of your own book is at pwlbtoday.org/loan-analysis, and the rates page at pwlbtoday.org/dashboard takes ten seconds to check.

One last piece for completeness. On the DMO's premature redemption curve at yesterday's PM fixing, our engine prices your 31-loan book at a substantial indicative discount driven mainly by two long-dated annuity positions at coupons of 2.15% and 2.22%. Your paragraph 8 states plainly that no rescheduling was done during the year, so this is context rather than a suggestion — break costs are indicative only, only the DMO can quote a binding settlement, and we do not model MRP or any accounting treatment.

On training, three look most relevant to Burnley. Interest rate risk, for the near-term rollover; Strategic PWLB borrowing, for the short-versus-long question your paragraph 5.2 discusses; and our Liability Benchmark pathway, which is interactive and built on live data — worth a look given where CIPFA is heading with the Prudential and Treasury Codes. You already ran member training in February (§3), and there's a members' course written for that same scrutiny role if it would help refresh. All 115 courses are free to local authorities until the end of September at pwlbtoday.org/academy, and free accounts for the whole team.

And if you do find it useful, mentioning it to others would help us more than anything. We're small, word of mouth is most of our marketing, and every sign-up helps us prove the need.

Sign up free → https://pwlbtoday.org/
Follow on LinkedIn → https://www.linkedin.com/company/pwlbtoday/

Russell
https://www.linkedin.com/in/russelltew
